fields.meta_title: Take a Free Career Quiz or Build Your Own | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Take a free career quiz that names the field of work your interests point to, then build one for your students or job seekers. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Career Quiz That Matches Interests to Fields of Work
fields.hero_description: Build a career quiz that sorts interests into fields of work and keeps every result in a database you own. Try the sample below.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Behind a Career Quiz
fields.features_subheading: A career quiz is a short set of questions whose answers point to a field of work. Emergent builds the quiz and what happens after it.
fields.feature_1:
Questions mapped to the results you name

Name the fields of work, programs, or jobs you want as results. Emergent builds the questions with each option pointing at one result, and changes any of them by prompt.
fields.feature_2:
Every finished quiz kept as a row

Each finished quiz becomes a row in a database you own, with the result, every option chosen, and a name or email if you ask for one. Filter by result before a class visit.
fields.feature_3:
Result screens tied to your catalog

Connect a course catalog or job board through its API and tag each program by field of work. The result screen then lists the programs or openings that carry the matching tag.
fields.feature_4:
A heads-up for whoever follows up

Pick who hears about each result: a counselor, an admissions advisor, or a coach. They get an email or a Slack message with the answers before they sit down with the quiz taker.
fields.feature_5:
One question per screen, no cap on takers

Takers answer one question per screen, on a phone in a hallway or a tablet at a job fair. Emergent puts no cap on responses, and a quiz sent to a whole district keeps every result.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain, and code you can keep

Publish the quiz on your school's or practice's own domain, included in Emergent and paid in credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository and keep a copy.

fields.tab_content_1:
When Elijah finishes, three trade electives appear

Fenwick Lake High School sends the career quiz to every junior in September. Elijah Tamsett lands on Building and Fixing, and his result screen lists the three trade electives tagged for that field: welding, construction, and auto technology. Counselor Joanna Venter has his answers by email before his October conference.
fields.tab_content_2:
A Health Sciences lead lands with its advisor

Cedar Plains Community College runs the career quiz on its admissions site, with a result for each program division. Lorena Wexler lands on Health Sciences and sees 3 certificate programs pulled from the catalog. Her lead goes by email to Calvin Rudd, the advisor for Health Sciences.
fields.tab_content_3:
Warren's answers are in before his Tuesday session

Every first booking with coach Simone Lacroix comes with the career quiz. Warren Ellery, a warehouse supervisor, finishes on Sunday with Data and Organizing and a salary floor of $64,000. Simone reads every answer in her inbox and opens Tuesday's session on two roles that fit: logistics analyst and inventory planner.
fields.tab_content_4:
Which employers to invite, counted from 640 results

At its spring job fair, Tallowford County Workforce Board runs the career quiz on tablets by the entrance. Of the 640 visitors who finished, 190 landed on Helping and Teaching and 170 on Building and Fixing. The board read the dashboard that week and invited more hospital and school district employers to the fall fair.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Career Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to make a career quiz whose results name a field of work and a next step for the person taking it.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Start with the decision the quiz feeds
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask about tasks, not job titles
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Hold it to eight to ten questions
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide what a taker should do after the result: pick an elective, apply to a program, or book a coaching session. That choice decides the results and who hears about each finished quiz. Write it down before the first question.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Choose four to six results named in plain words, like Building and Fixing or Helping and Teaching. Under each one, list three jobs or programs to look into. A result screen with nowhere to go next leaves the taker holding a label.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask which task sounds better, such as rebuilding a bike or planning a club budget, rather than which job title appeals. Write one option per result in every question, and keep each option the same length and tone as the others.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Eight to ten questions, one per screen, give every result room to win. That length still fits on a phone during a class period. Put profile questions, such as grade or current role, after the last scored question instead of at the start.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Write each result as a direction
fields.howto_step_5_des: Open each result with what the answers lean toward, such as hands-on work with tools. Then name three jobs and one next step, like a program to apply to or a person to talk with. Never tell a taker what they are or what they cannot do.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Send every result to a person
fields.howto_step_6_des: Decide who reads the answers: a counselor before a conference, an advisor for each program division, or a coach before a first session. Put that routing in your prompt, and Emergent builds the email alert along with the quiz and its database.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Play every path before you share it
fields.howto_step_7_des: Run through the quiz once per result, aiming at a different one each time, and check that each can win. Open the saved row and the email for every run. Send it to one homeroom or one cohort before the whole school sees it.

faq_plan.a: A career quiz asks about the tasks and settings you enjoy and scores your answers so they point to fields of work worth exploring. The O*NET Interest Profiler, a public example, measures six types of occupational interests. The quiz on this page asks eight questions and names one of six fields.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a career quiz?
faq_plan.a: List the results you want, such as fields of work or your own programs, and describe the quiz in a prompt, including what should happen after each result. Emergent's AI survey builder builds the questions and the database behind them. Publish it and share the link.

faq_plan.q: Can I make a free career quiz for my students?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Emergent is free to start, and the free tier covers building and publishing a career quiz for a class. Describe the grade, the fields of work you want as results, and who should read the answers, then send students the link.

faq_plan.q: What should a career quiz for adults ask that a student quiz skips?
faq_plan.a: Ask about work already done: the tasks from past jobs worth keeping, the ones to drop, and the lowest salary the person would accept. Put those after the scored questions so they add context without changing the result. The scoring works like a style quiz, where every option points to one result.

faq_plan.q: What questions belong in a career quiz for teens?
faq_plan.a: Ask about things a teenager has done: clubs, chores, and weekend jobs. Ask which part of a group project they would take, or whether they would rather fix a bike or design a poster. Keep the wording plain enough to finish on a phone in study hall.

faq_plan.q: What should a career path quiz show at the end?
faq_plan.a: It should show the field the answers lean toward, three jobs in that field, and one next step, such as a certificate program or a talk with an advisor. When you build it on Emergent, the app can connect to your course catalog through its API and list those programs on the result screen.

faq_plan.q: Can a career aptitude quiz score right and wrong answers?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if you build it that way. Give each question one correct option and map the total score to bands, the same setup as a vocabulary quiz. An interest quiz, like the one on this page, has no wrong answers, because each option points to a result instead.

faq_plan.q: How can I tell whether a free career quiz online is any good?
faq_plan.hint: How to choose a career quiz free?
faq_plan.a: Look at the questions first. Good ones ask about tasks and settings, not job titles. Then look at the result: it should name jobs to explore and a next step, not a personality label. Finally, check that the quiz says who made it and what happens to your answers.

faq_plan.q: Can a career quiz help me find work I enjoy?
faq_plan.hint: How to find your passion career quiz free?
faq_plan.a: It can narrow the search. A career quiz sorts what you already enjoy into a field of work and names jobs to look into, which gives you a short list to test. Treat the result as a starting point, and talk to someone in one of those jobs before deciding.

faq_plan.q: How can a career coach use a career quiz to find new clients?
faq_plan.hint: Is the princeton review career quiz free?
faq_plan.a: Put the quiz on a free trial landing page next to the offer of a first session at no charge, and send each result by email with a link to book. On Emergent, every taker's answers are saved to a database you own, and responses have no cap.

quiz.title: Career Quiz: Which Field of Work Fits You?
quiz.intro: Eight questions about the tasks you enjoy. Your result names the field of work your answers lean toward, with three jobs to look into and a next step.

questions.text: You have a free Saturday afternoon. Which plan sounds best?

options.text: Rebuild an old bike in the garage
Run a small experiment you read about
Paint, sketch, or edit a short video
Coach a younger kid's practice
Sell things at a weekend market
Sort out a messy closet or photo library

questions.text: Which school project would you pick first?

options.text: Design the poster and the slides
Lead the group and present the pitch
Build the model or the prototype
Track the budget and the deadlines
Interview people and write their stories
Research the question and test the answer

questions.text: A friend's laptop stops working. What do you do?

options.text: Look up the error and figure out the cause
Open it up and try to fix the part
Calm them down and help back up their files
Make a list of what to check, in order
Find the best repair deal and handle the call
Use the downtime to sketch on paper

questions.text: Which compliment would you like to hear most?

options.text: You are great at explaining things
You always know how things work
You can fix anything
You have a great eye
You get people moving
Nothing slips past you

questions.text: Where would you rather spend a workday?

options.text: Outdoors or in a workshop
In a lab or at a research desk
In a studio
In a classroom, clinic, or community center
In meetings and on calls with clients
At a desk with spreadsheets and systems

questions.text: Pick the class you would sign up for.

options.text: Business and marketing
Bookkeeping and spreadsheets
Woodshop or auto technology
Biology or chemistry
Graphic design or music
Child development or health

questions.text: Which problem would you most like to solve?

options.text: A bridge that needs a new support
Why a plant grows faster in one spot
A logo that does not look right
A neighbor who needs help getting to appointments
A shop that is losing customers
Records that do not add up

questions.text: What would make a job feel worth it to you?

options.text: Seeing something I built still standing
Finding an answer nobody had before
Making something people remember
Knowing I helped someone
Growing a team or a business
Running a system that never misses

results.title: Building and Fixing
results.description: Your answers lean toward hands-on work with tools, machines, and materials. Jobs to look into: electrician, HVAC technician, and civil engineering technician. Next step: take a shop or trades class, or shadow someone on a job site for a day.

results.title: Science and Research
results.description: Your answers lean toward asking why and testing ideas until you know. Jobs to look into: lab technician, environmental scientist, and software tester. Next step: take a lab science class or join a science fair project.

results.title: Arts and Design
results.description: Your answers lean toward making things that look, sound, or read well. Jobs to look into: graphic designer, video editor, and interior designer. Next step: start a portfolio with three pieces and ask someone in the field to review it.

results.title: Helping and Teaching
results.description: Your answers lean toward working with people and helping them get somewhere. Jobs to look into: teacher, nursing assistant, and social worker. Next step: volunteer with a school, clinic, or youth program for a few weeks.

results.title: Business and Leading
results.description: Your answers lean toward persuading people, running projects, and making deals. Jobs to look into: sales representative, marketing coordinator, and store manager. Next step: run a small project end to end, from a budget to a final pitch.

results.title: Data and Organizing
results.description: Your answers lean toward order, detail, and systems that run on time. Jobs to look into: bookkeeper, logistics analyst, and medical records specialist. Next step: learn spreadsheets well and offer to keep the records for a club or team.

plan.angle: The top 10 is free career quizzes run by issuers: a testing nonprofit, a test-prep company, state workforce sites, a university career office, a technical college system and a teaching nonprofit. None of them lets a visitor build one. This page gives a playable eight-question career quiz that sorts interests into six fields of work, then shows the people who run those quizzes (a high school counselor, a community college admissions office, a career coach and a county workforce board) what happens after the result: matching electives or programs on the result screen, an email to the advisor or coach, and a count of results that shapes the next job fair. The FAQ covers the free, adults, teens, career path and aptitude variants searchers type.
